notable_claims: Cornell University faced controversy and FBI involvement over illegal materials posted to alt.binaries.pictures.erotica.
Iowa State University implemented a three-tier Usenet access system (Focused, Standard, Full) to restrict certain groups.
Debate exists over whether restricting controversial newsgroups is a matter of academic freedom or prudent resource allocation.
Some university administrations view social email use as non-academic and potentially unsupported by taxpayer funding.
classification.summary: This digest summarizes discussions regarding Usenet access restrictions at various universities, specifically focusing on a child pornography controversy and FBI investigation at Cornell University. It examines the tension between academic freedom, resource allocation, and taxpayer accountability in state-run computing centers. Additionally, it lists specific acceptable use policies from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Louisiana Tech, University of North Texas, and University of Nebraska (Omaha).
classification.title: Abstract of CAF-News 02.59

notable_claims: The FBI searched a Cornell student's room and detained them for distributing child pornography.
Cornell had a reputation as the 'Bad Computing Center' of the world due to viruses and pornography.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding an FBI investigation and search of a student's room at Cornell University related to the distribution of child pornography via Usenet. The author defends the actions of system administrator Stuart Lynn and expresses a desire for Cornell to move past its reputation as a source of viruses and illicit content.

notable_claims: The ALA's 'Library Bill of Rights' suggests collections should be inclusive and cover sexual issues.
There is a distinction between academic resources provided by individuals versus those funded by public money in the context of academic freedom.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding Cornell University's decision to restrict access to erotica-related Usenet hierarchies. Participants debate whether such restrictions constitute censorship or a legitimate allocation of public funds and resources. Carl Kadie references American Library Association (ALA) guidelines on diversity and challenged materials to argue against broad bans.

notable_claims: Materials in libraries should not be removed under legal or extra-legal pressure if they meet selection criteria.
The 'best' way to minimize legal liability would result in the banning of all books, students, and computer newsgroups.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie responds to a discussion regarding Cornell University's access to erotica newsgroups by arguing against the minimization of legal liability as a primary institutional goal. He provides the American Library Association's policy on challenged materials to argue that content should only be banned after due process. The post emphasizes that academic institutions should protect freedom of expression despite potential legal pressures.

notable_claims: 18 USCS section 2252 defines child pornography as involving the use of a minor engaging in sexually explicit conduct.
Possession of more than three such visual depictions can lead to federal charges.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the legal definitions of child pornography in the context of FBI investigations into computer networks. The author cites 18 USCS section 2252 to clarify what constitutes illegal material and distribution on Netnews.

notable_claims: ISU implemented a tiered Usenet system restricting 'alt.' and 'rec.' groups on public machines.
The university justified restrictions as compliance with state and federal laws.
Access to unrestricted feeds required filing a form, which compromised user anonymity.
classification.summary: A report detailing the implementation of a three-tier Usenet access system at Iowa State University (ISU) that censored specific newsgroups. The policy restricted public-access machines to 'Standard' access and required students to file forms for full access, effectively removing anonymity. A student group called Students for Electronic Freedom advocated for user responsibility over administrative censorship.

notable_claims: University administration perceived student email as largely social and non-academic.
There was a concern that state legislators might cut funding if they believed university computing resources were being used for non-academic purposes.
classification.summary: Herb Stahlke of Ball State University discusses the tension between providing open network access and the fear that non-academic use (social email, newsgroups, games) could jeopardize state funding. He questions whether the perceived expectations of state legislators should influence university computing policy and practice. The post highlights the conflict between stewardship of public resources and academic freedom/privacy.
classification.title: State legislatures and acad-f policy

notable_claims: Concerns that state legislators may cut university funding if they perceive computer resources are used for non-academic purposes (e.g., games, newsgroups).
Open access to VAX clusters and email increases campus-wide computer literacy.
classification.summary: A discussion between a University Computing Services director and a community member regarding whether the fear of state legislature funding cuts should influence university network policies. Herb Stahlke argues that non-academic use of resources could lead to perceived mismanagement by taxpayers, while Andrew Templin argues against allowing politicians to dictate system usage, citing the benefits of computer literacy.

notable_claims: Computing equipment, software, files, and data are considered private property of individuals, organizations, or the Institute.
Accessing a user's private files during an investigation requires prior authorization from the Dean of Students (for students) or the Provost (for faculty/staff).
classification.summary: This item shares the official computing policy of Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (RPI). The policy defines computing facilities as community resources and private property, listing ten specific examples of misuse. It also outlines the administrative authorization required to investigate a user's private files.
classification.title: Policy: "USING COMPUTERS AT RENSSELAER"

notable_claims: Computer facilities and accounts are owned by the University and must be used for university-related activities only.
Electronic communications (MAIL) are restricted to university-related activities; fraudulent, harassing, or obscene messages are prohibited.
Copyrighted software may only be copied for backup purposes if permitted by the owner.
Violations of computer policies may be treated as criminal offenses under Louisiana Revised Statutes 14:73.
classification.summary: This item provides the text of the computer use policies at Louisiana Tech University. The policies mandate that computing facilities be used for university-related activities only and prohibit commercial use, unauthorized account sharing, and copyright infringement. It outlines a disciplinary process for violations, ranging from loss of privileges to dismissal or legal action.
classification.title: Louisiana Tech University Computer Policies

notable_claims: Access to University computer resources is considered a privilege granted by the University.
University computer resources shall be used solely for legitimate University-related purposes.
All computerized institutional data is considered an asset of the University.
classification.summary: This document outlines the 'Computer Resources Security Policy' for the University of North Texas. It defines computer resources broadly to include centrally administered, departmental, and personal computers, asserting that access is a privilege rather than a right. The policy mandates that university resources be used solely for legitimate university-related purposes and establishes a hierarchy of security roles including stewards, custodians, and guardians.

notable_claims: Violations of computer policy may be subject to Nebraska State Statutes Chapters 28-1343 and 86-707.
University accounts issued for classroom or office work must not be used for private consulting or personal financial gain.
organizations: Office of Computing and Data Communications
classification.summary: This item provides the official computer and network use policies for the University of Nebraska at Omaha (UNO). The policy outlines standards of conduct, prohibits unauthorized access to data, and forbids using university accounts for personal financial gain. It establishes that violations may be governed by student/faculty handbooks and state statutes.
